tasks.prompt: Maya Rodriguez wants to work from Portugal for 42 calendar days, 5 October to 15 November 2026. Can she? Check her profile and rolling international usage, retrieve the international and remote-work policies, and explain the limit and any compliant options with citations.

trace.question: Maya Rodriguez wants to work from Portugal for 42 calendar days, 5 October to 15 November 2026. Can she? Check her profile and rolling international usage, retrieve the international and remote-work policies, and explain the limit and any compliant options with citations.
trace.answer:
**No – Maya cannot work from Portugal for the full 42 calendar days as requested.**  

**Why the request exceeds policy**

1. **Rolling 30‑day limit** – The International Remote Work policy allows a maximum of 30 calendar days of work abroad in any rolling 12‑month period. Maya has already used 12 days (Ireland, March 2‑13 2026), leaving only 18 days remaining (POL‑INTL‑001 §2 The 30‑Day Rule; usage citation POL‑INTL‑001 §2 Rolling 30‑Day Limit).  

2. **Country‑specific cap** – Portugal is an eligible country, but the maximum consecutive days allowed there is 30 (POL‑INTL‑001 §3 Eligible Countries).  

3. **Requested duration** – Maya’s request (Oct 5 – Nov 15 2026) is 42 days, exceeding both the overall 30‑day rolling limit and Portugal’s 30‑day cap (POL‑INTL‑001 §2 The 30‑Day Rule).  

**Compliant alternatives**

| Option | How it fits policy | Required steps |
|--------|-------------------|----------------|
| **Reduce the stay to ≤ 30 days** (e.g., Oct 5 – Nov 3) | Meets both the rolling limit (18 days available) and Portugal’s 30‑day cap. | Submit an International Remote Work request ≥ 20 business days before the start date (POL‑INTL‑001 §4 Approval Workflow). |
| **Take the excess 12 days as PTO or unpaid leave** (work 30 days, then 12 days off) | Excess days must be taken as approved PTO/unpaid leave with no work performed (POL‑INTL‑001 §2). | Request PTO for the 12 days through Workday; ensure manager and HR approval. |
| **Pursue a permanent relocation** | Allows work beyond 30 days but requires a new employment agreement and 90‑day lead time (POL‑INTL‑001 §4). | Initiate a relocation request with Global Mobility; provide 90‑day notice. |
| **Apply for a short‑term international assignment** | Sponsored assignments can exceed the 30‑day limit with VP approval (POL‑INTL‑001 §4). | Business unit submits assignment proposal; obtain VP and Global Mobility sign‑off. |

**Next steps**  
Maya should either shorten the Portugal stay to 30 days or split the period, using PTO for the remaining days. If she needs the full 42 days for business reasons, she must explore relocation or a short‑term assignment as outlined above. All requests must follow the approval workflow in POL‑INTL‑001 §4.

hits.doc_title: International Remote Work and Tax Compliance Policy
hits.text:
An approved employee may work from an eligible country for a maximum of 30 calendar days per rolling 12-month period , across all
  countries combined. Days are counted as calendar days present in the country
  while performing any work, including partial days.

Requests exceeding 30 days are not approved as temporary international
  remote work . An employee who needs to work abroad for longer than 30
  days must either:

- take the excess period as approved PTO or unpaid leave, performing no work
      whatsoever during that period; or
- pursue a permanent relocation through Global Mobility, which requires an
      entity in the destination country, a new employment agreement, and a
      minimum lead time of 90 days ; or
- be assigned to a formal short-term international assignment, which is
      sponsored by the business unit and requires VP approval.

A six-week (42-day) request, for example, exceeds the 30-day limit and cannot
  be approved as ordinary international remote work.

hits.doc_title: International Remote Work and Tax Compliance Policy
hits.text:
Temporary international remote work is permitted only in countries where
  Helios has assessed the tax and permanent-establishment risk. As of the
  effective date, the eligible list is:

| Country | Max consecutive days | Notes |
| Ireland | 30 | Helios entity present |
| Portugal | 30 | Helios entity present |
| Spain | 21 | No entity; PE risk after 21 days |
| Italy | 21 | No entity; PE risk after 21 days |
| Germany | 21 | No entity; PE risk after 21 days |
| Netherlands | 21 | No entity; PE risk after 21 days |
| United Kingdom | 30 | Treaty relief available |
| Canada | 30 | Ontario and British Columbia only |
| Mexico | 14 | Immigration restrictions |
| Singapore | 30 | Helios entity present |
| Japan | 14 | Immigration restrictions |

Work from any country not on this list is prohibited without a
  case-by-case assessment by Global Mobility & Tax, which requires a minimum
  of 20 business days to complete. Work from countries subject
  to sanctions or export-control restrictions is prohibited outright; see POL-SEC-001 Section 8.

An employee may work temporarily from a US location other than their registered
address without changing their work arrangement, subject to duration limits:

| Duration | Approval required | Additional requirements |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 – 10 consecutive business days | Manager notification only | None |
| 11 – 20 consecutive business days | Manager written approval | Security review under `POL-SEC-001` §7 |
| 21 – 30 consecutive business days | Manager + HR Business Partner | Security review + payroll notification |
| More than 30 consecutive days in a state where the employee is not registered | Not permitted as temporary work | Requires a permanent work-location change under Section 4 |

The **30-day rule** exists because working more than 30 days in a state creates
state income-tax withholding and, in some states, employer-registration
obligations. Cumulative days in the same state within a rolling 12-month period
count toward the 30-day threshold.

Helios Systems supports flexible work arrangements where they are compatible
with the employee's role, team needs, and legal obligations. This policy defines
the available work arrangements, who is eligible for each, and how to request a
change.

Temporary work from a location outside the employee's home country is governed
by `POL-INTL-001` (International Remote Work and Tax Compliance) and requires
additional approvals.

hits.doc_title: International Remote Work and Tax Compliance Policy
hits.text:
1. Employee submits an International Remote Work request in Helios Workday at
      least 20 business days before the intended start date,
      specifying destination country, exact dates, and total calendar days.
2. Manager approval — confirms coverage and time-zone overlap
      under POL-REMOTE-001 Section 8.
3. Global Mobility & Tax review — confirms the country is
      eligible, the day count is within limits, and no permanent-establishment
      or payroll-withholding trigger applies.
4. Immigration check — confirms the employee holds the right
      to be present and, where required, the right to work. Employees on a US
      work visa (including H-1B, L-1, O-1, and TN status) must additionally be
      cleared by Immigration Counsel, as travel may affect status or re-entry.
5. Information Security review — required for all
      international requests, per POL-SEC-001 Section 7.
6. Written approval is issued in Workday. No travel should be booked
      before written approval is issued.

Typical end-to-end approval time is 10 – 20 business days. Requests submitted
  with less than 20 business days' notice are reviewed on a best-effort basis and
  are frequently denied for lack of review time.

|-------------------|------------------------|

Your request is for **3 consecutive business days** (Sept 21‑23 2026). According to the bands, the required notice is **10 business days**, not 20. The 20‑day requirement applies only to absences of 6–10 consecutive business days.

**Citations**

* `check_policy_compliance` notice_bands: 3–5 days → 10 business days (see the `notice_bands` array in the compliance output).

hits.text:
Advance notice requirements scale with the length of the absence:

| Length of absence | Minimum advance notice |
| --- | --- |
| 1 – 2 consecutive business days | 3 business days |
| 3 – 5 consecutive business days | 10 business days |
| 6 – 10 consecutive business days | 20 business days |
| More than 10 consecutive business days | 30 business days, plus skip-level approval |

Requests submitted with less than the minimum notice are not automatically
denied, but require documented manager approval and a stated business
justification.

1. The employee submits a PTO request in Helios Workday, specifying start date,
   end date, and total hours.
2. The request routes to the employee's direct manager of record.
3. The manager approves or denies within **3 business days**. If a manager does
   not respond within 3 business days, the request escalates automatically to
   the skip-level manager.
4. Approved requests are deducted from the PTO balance on the first day of the
   absence, not at the time of approval.

Employees must not book non-refundable travel before receiving written approval.

Absences of **four (4) or more consecutive days** due to the employee's own
serious health condition are handled under this policy rather than PTO
(`POL-PTO-001`, Section 7). Absences of one to three days are ordinary sick
absences charged to PTO.

In addition to the observed holidays above, each full-time employee receives
**two (2) floating holidays** per calendar year, credited on January 1.

- Floating holidays may be used for any purpose, including religious or cultural
  observances not on the company schedule.
- Floating holidays require the same advance notice as a 1 – 2 day PTO request
  (3 business days; see `POL-PTO-001`, Section 3.1).
- Floating holidays **do not carry over** and are forfeited if unused by
  December 31.
- Floating holidays are **not paid out** at separation.
- Employees hired after July 1 receive one (1) floating holiday for that year.

Part-time employees receive one (1) floating holiday per calendar year.

Helios operates a combined PTO bank; there is no separate sick-time balance for
absences of 1 – 3 days. Absences of **4 or more consecutive days** due to the
employee's own serious health condition are handled under `POL-LEAVE-002`
(Parental and Medical Leave) and are not charged to PTO.

Employees should notify their manager as early as possible on the first day of
an unplanned sick absence. No advance notice is required for sick absences.

trace.question: What is the maximum number of consecutive days I may work from another country?
trace.answer:
You may work from an overseas location for **up to 30 calendar days** in any rolling 12‑month period, counted across all countries combined. If you stay longer you must use PTO, unpaid leave, or pursue a permanent relocation or formal assignment (POL‑INTL‑001 §2 The 30‑Day Rule).

In addition, each eligible country has its own maximum consecutive‑day limit. For example, Spain, Italy, Germany, the Netherlands, and a few others are limited to **21 consecutive days**, while many countries (Ireland, Portugal, United Kingdom, Canada, Singapore, etc.) allow the full **30 consecutive days** (POL‑INTL‑001 §3 Eligible Countries).  

So the overall ceiling is 30 days, but you must also respect the per‑country cap shown in the eligible‑countries table.

trace.question: Is Sofia Marino covered by short-term disability? Explain why or why not.
trace.answer:
No. Sofia Marino is **not covered by short‑term disability**.

**Reasoning**  
Sofia’s employee record shows she is a part‑time employee (24 hours/week). The Benefits Eligibility matrix lists short‑term disability as a benefit **only for full‑time employees** and explicitly “No” for part‑time staff (POL‑BEN‑001 §3 Eligibility Matrix). The Short‑Term Disability section of the Parental and Medical Leave policy reiterates that “Part‑time employees are not covered by short‑term disability” (POL‑LEAVE‑002 §3.2 Short‑Term Disability). Sofia’s benefits status also records short‑term disability as false with the same citation.

**Citations**  
- POL‑BEN‑001 §3 Eligibility Matrix – short‑term disability: Yes for full‑time, No for part‑time.  
- POL‑LEAVE‑002 §3.2 Short‑Term Disability – “Part‑time employees are not covered by short‑term disability.”

hits.text:
A change in employment type that affects eligibility is a qualifying life event.
Benefits change on the effective date of the employment-type change, not the
date of the request. An employee moving from full-time to part-time loses
short-term and long-term disability coverage and moves to the employee-only
medical subsidy.

Full-time employees are covered by employer-paid short-term disability:

| Period | Benefit |
| --- | --- |
